governance_justification: No AI statute is in force: binding AI-relevant duties come mainly from cross-sector data protection law (NDPA s 37, GAID Art 43) plus narrow sectoral rules (SEC robo-advisory rules, NCC Internet Code of Practice s 5.4), while AI-specific direction comes from the 2025 National AI Strategy and a pending bill.
institutional_map: The NDPC is the main cross-sector enforcer over AI today, through the NDPA 2023 and GAID 2025 (automated-decision safeguards, DPIAs and filings, sanctions). Sector regulators hold narrower AI-relevant powers: the SEC enforces its 2021 robo-advisory rules on algorithm governance, bias testing and annual independent technology audits; the NCC's Internet Code of Practice 2026 requires internet access providers to notify it and affected subscribers before deploying AI tools; and on 6 July 2026 the FCCPC, on presidential directive, opened an investigation under the FCCPA 2018 into Meta, Alphabet, X and generative-AI platforms. The Federal Ministry of Communications, Innovation and Digital Economy owns AI policy and published the Strategy, which looks to NITDA to promote an AI governance system; NITDA has no AI-specific enforcement power yet but would become the AI 'Regulatory Agency' under the pending Bill, overlapping with the NDPC and NCC. On 7 July 2026 the Minister reportedly told the NCC, NITDA and NDPC to defer enforcing recently issued platform rules under harmonisation and set up a joint committee to recommend a harmonised framework; whether this reaches the NCC code's AI provisions is unclear. Separate AI bills are before the National Assembly; none has been enacted.
conv: As on the EU plate and others built on GDPR-style law, Nigeria's binding AI layer runs through data protection: a right not to be subject to solely automated decisions (NDPA s 37) and mandatory impact assessments, filed with the regulator, for profiling, automated decisions and AI deployments (GAID Arts 28, 43).

As on several other plates in the atlas, strategy comes before statute, and the pending bill borrows the EU AI Act's vocabulary: an OECD-style definition of 'AI system', risk-proportionate obligations, accredited auditors and regulatory sandboxes.
gaps: Outside data protection, binding AI rules exist only in narrow sectors (SEC robo-advice, NCC network AI tools), so models built on non-personal or anonymised data, and model-level risks, fall outside any cross-sector enforceable rule until the Digital Economy and E-Governance Bill is enacted.

Affected people are told that automated decisions exist and of their significance and consequences, but have no right to the logic of an individual decision; and AI oversight is split among the NDPC, NCC, SEC, FCCPC and a future NITDA regulator with no statutory coordination mechanism, only a ministry-led, non-statutory harmonisation process begun in July 2026.
assume: One team (Solo) contributed five rows; all are kept and re-verified against official text. Excluded: the team's own exclusions (2022 NITDA platform code, draft NITDA AI code, NBA and Lagos AI guidelines, House AI bills) and two binding sectoral instruments the team did not code, the SEC Rules on Robo-Advisory Services (2021) and the NCC Internet Code of Practice 2026 (s 5.4); these are reflected in Part B only. The GAID is coded Binding as subordinate rules under NDPA ss 61-62. The team coded the model Soft-law-led; the editors changed it to Hybrid because the binding layer is wider than data protection. The team's recorded dilemma was whether to code the E-Governance Bill's risk classification as Present on press reports; the official text shows s 65 only empowers NITDA to set risk classes later and names no tiers, so it is coded Absent. The Bill's stage and the July 2026 ministerial deferral rest on press reports; no Senate passage or assent was found. No translation was needed. Status verified as of 19-11-2026.

instruments.name: Nigeria Data Protection Act 2023
instruments.systems: Any processing of personal data, by automated means or not, which captures AI systems that process personal data; AI is never named
instruments.trigger: Processing personal data where the controller or processor operates in Nigeria, the processing occurs in Nigeria, or the data subject is in Nigeria (s 2)
instruments.duties: Transparency; Impact assessment; Data governance; Registration or filing
instruments.duty_note: Tell data subjects about processing, including any automated decision-making; run a DPIA before high-risk processing; apply processing principles and security; register if of major importance (ss 24, 27-28, 39, 44)
instruments.remedy: NDPC enforcement orders, including compensation and penalties up to the greater of N10m or 2% of prior-year gross revenue (major importance) or N2m or 2% (others) (s 48); offence of ignoring a compliance order, fine or up to 1 year's imprisonment (s 49); civil damages (s 51)
instruments.gap: The Act never mentions AI and does not separate developers from deployers, so it reaches AI only through personal-data processing and leaves AI built on anonymised or non-personal data outside its duties.
instruments.citation: Nigeria Data Protection Act 2023 (Act No 37), Official Gazette No 119, Vol 110 (1 July 2023), ss 2, 24, 27, 28, 44, 48

instruments.name: Nigeria Data Protection Act 2023, s 37 (automated decision-making)
instruments.systems: Decisions based solely on automated processing of personal data, including profiling, that produce legal or similarly significant effects
instruments.trigger: A controller takes a decision about a data subject based solely on automated processing with legal or similarly significant effects
instruments.duty_note: Controllers must put safeguards in place, including human intervention, a chance for the person to give their view, and a way to contest the decision (s 37(3))
instruments.remedy: Borrowed from the same Act: NDPC enforcement orders and penalties (s 48; up to the greater of N10m or 2% of prior-year gross revenue for major-importance controllers), offence of ignoring a compliance order (s 49), civil damages (s 51)
instruments.gap: The right is an opt-out with wide exceptions (contract, written law, consent), and although ss 27(1)(g) and 34 require notice of the significance and consequences of automated decisions, nothing gives the person the logic of their own decision, so they contest outcomes they cannot see into.
instruments.citation: Nigeria Data Protection Act 2023 (Act No 37), s 37; see also ss 27(1)(g), 34(1)(a)(viii)

instruments.name: Nigeria Data Protection Act General Application and Implementation Directive (GAID) 2025
instruments.systems: Emerging technologies 'such as Artificial Intelligence, Internet of Things and Blockchain' used to process personal data, plus profiling and automated decisions (Arts 28, 43-44)
instruments.trigger: Deploying or planning to deploy AI or other emerging technologies to process personal data; listed DPIAs must be filed before processing starts (Arts 28(3), 28(9), 43); issued 20 March 2025, applied from 19 September 2025
instruments.duties: Risk management; Impact assessment; Data governance; Registration or filing; Prohibition
instruments.duty_note: Document design parameters, run a DPIA covering disparate outcomes, test in low-risk settings, monitor continuously, file with the annual compliance audit return, and stop using systems that cannot comply with human-rights law (Arts 43-44(3))
instruments.remedy: None of its own; relies on NDPA Part X (s 48), and a failed DPIA may also lead to restriction of the controller's platforms (Art 28(6))
instruments.gap: AI appears only as an example of 'emerging technologies', with no definition or threshold; the core design duty is phrased as an expectation (Art 43(2)) and the duty to stop using a system turns on the controller's own judgement (Art 44(3)), so it is unclear when an AI deployment crosses the line.
instruments.citation: Nigeria Data Protection Commission, Nigeria Data Protection Act General Application and Implementation Directive 2025 (NDPC/NDP ACT-GAID/01/2025, 20 March 2025), arts 8-9, 28, 40, 43-44

instruments.name: National Artificial Intelligence Strategy
instruments.systems: AI across the economy; five pillars, including responsible and ethical AI and a robust AI governance framework
instruments.trigger: None; a 'living document' setting strategies to be implemented over five years
instruments.duty_note: No legal duties; commits government to national AI principles, an AI governance regulatory body, a national AI policy framework and an AI risk-management framework (strategies 5.1.1-5.1.4)
instruments.enf: None named; the Ministry leads, with an AI governance regulatory system to be promoted by NITDA
instruments.gap: It promises principles, a risk-management framework and an AI governance regulatory body but creates no enforceable duty, right or sanction, so delivery depends on legislation and NITDA instruments that are not yet in force.
instruments.citation: Federal Ministry of Communications, Innovation and Digital Economy, National Artificial Intelligence Strategy (September 2025)

instruments.name: National Digital Economy and E-Governance Bill 2025
instruments.systems: Any AI system developed, deployed, placed on the market or used in Nigeria, by private persons or public institutions; NITDA may classify AI by risk through later regulation (ss 2(d), 63-65, 83)
instruments.trigger: Developing, deploying, marketing, operating or making available an AI system used or relied on in Nigeria (s 83); would apply only on enactment, and no Senate passage or assent had been reported by 19-11-2026
instruments.duties: Transparency; Risk management; Impact assessment; Audit; Human oversight; Data governance
instruments.duty_note: AI agents must apply risk-proportionate governance, risk-management and impact-assessment measures, inform affected persons, reduce bias, keep audit-ready records and allow human intervention where rights face significant risk (ss 63-64)
instruments.enf: National Information Technology Development Agency (NITDA), as the 'Regulatory Agency', cooperating with the NDPC (ss 64(1)(j), 66-68, 83)
instruments.remedy: Enforcement orders to remedy, compensate, account for profits or pay up to the higher of N10m or 2% of prior-year Nigerian gross revenue; suspension of seriously risky systems; civil liability (ss 67-68)
instruments.gap: The Bill leaves the risk classes and most detailed obligations to future NITDA regulations, and while it tells AI agents to cooperate with the NDPC it sets no mechanism for resolving clashes between NITDA, the NDPC and sectoral regulators.
instruments.citation: National Digital Economy and E-Governance Bill 2025 (National Assembly), Pt XI ss 63-69, Pt XII ss 70-79, s 83
